newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish truce holds amid looming talks tension.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish truce holds amid looming talks tension.

text.p: Northern Ireland was reported quiet after IRA guerrillas formally halted their guerrilla war against British rule to gain a voice in peace talks.

Sinn Fein, the Irish Republican Army's political wing, said the start of the ceasefire at midday on Sunday marked "a momentous day," following 28 years of sectarian and political conflict that cost 3,200 lives.

But angry pro-British Unionists accused Britain of winning a truce, which Protestant politicians believe will prove to be simply cosmetic, by backsliding on a key demand for the surrender of IRA weapons.

British Prime Minister Tony Blair was to meet powerful Protestant leader David Trimble in London on Monday to try to keep his Ulster Unionist Party within a peace process now set to be joined by Sinn Fein.

"Tony Blair has fallen for the line that if you get the IRA into talks, you will be able to test the colour and value of their money. That is not the case," Ken Maginnis, a close colleague of Trimble, told Reuters.

"Very clearly it is tactical, it is a phoney ceasefire. It is simply the IRA trying to extract concessions from a government that they are currently testing..." Peter Robinson, of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP), told Sky Television.
As darkness fell on Sunday, police said there had been no attacks on security forces. "Since midday there have been no terrorist or paramilitary incidents," a police spokesman said.
In the town of Lurgan where IRA activists shot dead two police officers last month, about 2,000 Protestants and Catholics held an open-air vigil and embraced each other in symbol of peace.
They were commemorating Bernadette Martin, an 18-year-old Catholic who became the most recent victim in a long catalogue of sectarian murders when she was shot a week ago as she slept in bed.
The IRA said it had stood down all its units and was unequivocally restoring a ceasefire of August 1994 which collapsed after 18 months.
Two extremist splinter groups, the Irish National Liberation Army and the Continuity Army Council which attacked British security forces, made no comment on the IRA's decision.
Unionists, who want Northern Ireland to stay British, are riled that Sinn Fein is set to join all-party peace talks and meet British ministers while the IRA keeps its guns and bombs.

Although not yet admitted to round-table talks, Sinn Fein leaders will go to the east Belfast talks venue on Monday and say they expect to be allowed to use office facilities already set aside for them.
But Robinson said the DUP might stay away from the venue. "I think if it is contaminated by the presence of the Provisional IRA's representatives, it is unlikely that we will be there," he said.
The DUP says it will refuse to enter September negotiations with Sinn Fein unless the IRA disarms.
Trimble, who will press Blair to toughen his stance on IRA weapons, has not yet said if he will side with the rival DUP in what would be a further blow to talks that have limped along for 13 months.
Sinn Fein, which was barred from current multi-party talks because of IRA attacks, could enter full round-table talks on September 15 if the truce holds.
